'''Ferruccio Ritossa''' (February 25, 1936 – January 9, 2014) was an Italian [[geneticist]] best known for his discovery of the [[heat shock response]] in the [[model organism]] ''[[Drosophila]]'' (fruit flies).<ref name="capocci_2014">{{cite journal |last1=Capocci |first1=Mauro |last2=Santoro |first2=M. Gabriella |last3=Hightower |first3=Lawrence E. |title=The life and times of Ferruccio Ritossa |journal=Cell Stress and Chaperones |date=September 2014 |volume=19 |issue=5 |pages=599–604 |doi=10.1007/s12192-014-0525-4 |pmc=4147064|pmid=25142515 |doi-access=free }}</ref><ref name="majno_2004">{{cite book |last1=Majno |first1=Guido |last2=Joris |first2=Isabelle |title=Cells, tissues, and disease : principles of general pathology |date=2004 |publisher=Oxford University Press |location=New York |isbn=9780199748921 |page=187 |edition=2nd |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=8yAf6U7njlcC&pg=PA187}}</ref> 

==Early life and education==
Ritossa was born in the town of [[Pinguente]] in [[Istria]] in 1936, one of three sons. His father, a butcher, was killed in the [[foibe killings]] when Ritossa was a young child.<ref name=capocci_2014 /><ref name="capocci_2016">{{cite web |last1=Capocci |first1=Mauro |title=Ritossa, Ferruccio |url=https://www.treccani.it/enciclopedia/ferruccio-ritossa_(Dizionario-Biografico)/ |website=Biographical Dictionary of Italians |date=2016}}</ref> His mother moved the family to Italy and taught school in an orphanage, where her three children were also educated. Ritossa attended the [[University of Bologna]] to study agricultural sciences and graduated in 1958.<ref name=capocci_2014 /> He became interested in [[genetics]], particularly in then-emerging molecular studies of the field, and joined a newly established course in [[biophysics]] taught by [[Adriano Buzzati-Traverso]] at the [[University of Pavia]], where Buzzati-Traverso had begun to establish ''[[Drosophila]]'' research and collections. Buzzati-Traverso founded a laboratory, now the [[Istituto di Genetica e Biofisica]], in [[Naples]] and invited Ritossa to join him there.<ref name=capocci_2014 /><ref name="demaio_2012">{{cite journal |last1=De Maio |first1=Antonio |last2=Santoro |first2=M. Gabriella |last3=Tanguay |first3=Robert M. |last4=Hightower |first4=Lawrence E. |title=Ferruccio Ritossa's scientific legacy 50 years after his discovery of the heat shock response: a new view of biology, a new society, and a new journal |journal=Cell Stress and Chaperones |date=March 2012 |volume=17 |issue=2 |pages=139–143 |doi=10.1007/s12192-012-0320-z|pmid=22252402 |pmc=3273555 |doi-access=free }}</ref>

==Heat shock studies==
Ritossa was interested in the newly emerging field of [[molecular genetics]] and began to study the [[polytene chromosome]]s found in ''Drosophila'' [[salivary gland]]s. These chromosomes exhibit characteristic changes called "puffs" under certain conditions, now known to reflect activation of [[transcription (genetics)|transcription]].<ref name=capocci_2014 /><ref name=majno_2004 /> As Ritossa later recalled,<ref name="ritossa_1996">{{cite journal |last1=Ritossa |first1=F |title=Discovery of the heat shock response. |journal=Cell Stress & Chaperones |date=June 1996 |volume=1 |issue=2 |pages=97–8 |pmid=9222594|pmc=248460 }}</ref> an accidental change in the temperature of a laboratory incubator unexpectedly revealed a distinct "puffing" pattern, and in following up on this [[serendipitous]] discovery he found that [[RNA]] was reliably and rapidly produced in puffs induced by temperature, later described as "the first known environmental stress acting directly on gene activity".<ref name=capocci_2014 /> The paper describing these observations was reportedly rejected by the high-impact [[scientific journal]] ''[[Nature (journal)|Nature]]''<ref name=capocci_2014 /> and eventually published in the journal ''[[Experientia]]'' in 1962.<ref name="ritossa_1962">{{cite journal |last1=Ritossa |first1=F. |title=A new puffing pattern induced by temperature shock and DNP in drosophila |journal=Experientia |date=December 1962 |volume=18 |issue=12 |pages=571–573 |doi=10.1007/BF02172188|s2cid=32525462 }}</ref> The paper was not initially widely cited.<ref name=capocci_2014 /><ref name=demaio_2012 /> Its significance became more widely appreciated in the 1970s as new information emerged, particularly with the discovery of [[heat shock protein]]s reported in 1974<ref name="tissieres_1974">{{cite journal |last1=Tissiéres |first1=Alfred |last2=Mitchell |first2=Herschel K. |last3=Tracy |first3=Ursula M. |title=Protein synthesis in salivary glands of Drosophila melanogaster: Relation to chromosome puffs |journal=Journal of Molecular Biology |date=April 1974 |volume=84 |issue=3 |pages=389–398 |doi=10.1016/0022-2836(74)90447-1|pmid=4219221 }}</ref> and the identification of heat-shock responses in other organisms, now recognized as a universal response.<ref name=capocci_2014 /><ref name=demaio_2012 />

==Subsequent career==
Ritossa spent several years working in the United States, first working with [[Robert von Borstel]] at [[Oak Ridge National Laboratory]] and later with [[Sol Spiegelman]] and [[Kimball C. Atwood III|Kim Atwood]] at the [[University of Illinois]].<ref name=capocci_2014 /> He returned to Italy to rejoin Buzzati-Traverso's laboratory institution in Naples and remained there till 1969, when he joined the faculty at the [[University of Bari]]. After 15 years he moved again to the [[University of Bologna]], from which he retired in the 1990s.<ref name=capocci_2014 /> Although he was for some time better known for his work on [[nucleic acid hybridization]] with Spiegelman and Atwood than for heat shock, growing interest in the field recognized his contributions, including through a 1982 meeting at [[Cold Spring Harbor Laboratory]] that was the first specifically on heat shock.<ref name=capocci_2014 /><ref name=demaio_2012 /> He was recognized with a medal by the [[Cell Stress Society International]],<ref name="cssi">{{cite web |title=Ferruccio Ritossa, Sculptor, CSSI Medalist & Distinguished Lifetime Member |url=https://cellstressresponses.org/news/ferruccio-ritossa-sculptor/ |website=CSSI |access-date=16 January 2021}}</ref> which now maintains an award for early-career scientists in his honor.<ref name="cssi_award">{{cite web |title=Ferruccio Ritossa Early Career Award |url=https://cellstressresponses.org/ritossa/ |website=CSSI |access-date=16 January 2021}}</ref>

==Retirement==
After retiring from his faculty position, Ritossa moved to a farm near [[Dozza]] and became a [[sculptor]].<ref name=capocci_2014 /><ref name=demaio_2012 /><ref name=cssi /> He died on January 9, 2014.<ref name=capocci_2014 />
